name: Baure
confidence_why: Danielsen (2007), the only modern phonological description, puts Baure stress on the second syllable from the left with vowel weight deciding disyllables and endorses Baptista and Wallin's (1968) second-syllable finding; the sole dissent, Maggio's 1749 missionary grammar with its "usually penultimate, often antepenultimate, sometimes final", is older, gives no conditioning and largely matches that same pattern counted from the right, so the reading is clear but rests on few sources and on Danielsen's own hedges.

Maggio 1749/1880, Gramática Cap. I 'Del Acento y Declinación', p. 1 (= PDF leaf 14; also quoted in Danielsen's fn. 88, p. 64). Admiraal 2016: 76.
catalog_quote: Stress is not contrastive in Baure. ... It has been argued that stress appears on the penultimate syllable (Magio 1749 in Adam & Leclerc 1880: 1). Baptista & Wallin, on the other hand, came to the conclusion that "stress most frequently is found on the second syllable" (1968: 7, T-562: 22). The last statement can be judged to be correct, even though it is a generalization that will be specified here. The stress patterns are very difficult to generalize in fact, as they depend on the length of the word, the type of syllable, and last but not least, on the type of morpheme. ... First of all, there is generally only one stress in a word. When the word is longer than four syllables there is secondary stress, which cannot occur on an adjacent syllable. ... In these words we find the pattern of stressing the second syllable quite regularly. [Danielsen 2007: 64] ... The stress rules are more complex when they concern disyllabic nouns. ... the different vowels have different syllable weight. A stress shift to the first (or penultimate) syllable can be observed when the last syllable is especially light with a weak vowel. Weak vowels are /o/ and /i/ ... stress of the second syllable when it contains the vowels /a/ or /e/, in a less common constellation heavy /i/ and the diphthong /oe/, which is also heavy. The first syllable is stressed in all words which contain the vowels /o/ or weak /i/ in the last syllable, which undergoes vowel elision or palatalization. [Danielsen 2007: 65]
world_status: statement found in an open source

Antonio Magio de la Compañía de Jesus.. en las reducciones de la Concepcion, S. Martin, y S. Nicolas.. año 1749", then "Capítulo I. Del Acento y Declinacion." followed verbatim by "El acento suele tenerlo en la penúltima silaba, bastantes veces en la antepenúltima, y algunas en la última." The same sentence appears in both IA scanned files ( line 257; line 477). Two trivial correctio…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default penultimate word accent, with a sizeable set of antepenultimate words and a few final-accented ones; the source gives no conditioning for the exceptions. Modern support for penultimate default: Admiraal 2016: 76 says primary stress in compounds falls on the (usually penultimate syllable of the) locative noun stem and occurs once per phonological word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in Maggio 1749/1880; Admiraal 2016: 76 notes that in a compound only one primary stress occurs, whereas in a possessive noun phrase both nouns carry stress.
new_statements.exceptions: 'bastantes veces en la antepenúltima, y algunas en la última' — frequent antepenultimate and occasional final accent, unexplained; later (Gramática ~p. 13) the reciprocal suffix sequence -bobo is said to carry the accent on its first bo.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms in a missionary grammar, 1749 Baure, i.e. the historical variety); 'acento' in the 18th-century Jesuit tradition = stress. Modern Baure has extensive final-vowel elision (Baptista & Wallin 1968), so surface stress position in the modern language is expected to differ from this description; the authoritative modern statement is in Danielsen 2007 (phonology ch., pp. 61–81 per Admiraal), which could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes 18th-century mission Baure (Maggio, Concepción/San Martín/San Nicolás reductions, 1749), edited by Adam & Leclerc 1880; the modern language documented by Danielsen (Baure proper, with Carmelito dialect and the near-extinct Joaquiniano, all under baur1253) has undergone heavy final-vowel elision, so the surface stress facts may differ. Admiraal 2016 (modern Baure) independently indicates penultimate default stress at word level.

new_statements.relation_note: Danielsen explicitly cites the Maggio 1749 penultimate statement that the catalog records and rejects it in favour of Baptista & Wallin's 'second syllable' generalisation, refined by weight: for words of three or more syllables stress falls on the second syllable from the left (= penult only in trisyllables, antepenult in quadrisyllables), and in disyllables the position depends on the weight of the final vowel. So the catalog's 'fixed: penultimate' is contradicted as a rule, although Maggio's own wording (penult usually, often antepenult, sometimes final) is not incompatible with a second-syllable-from-the-left pattern seen from the right edge. Danielsen also adds that stress is not contra…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive. The default is the second syllable of the phonological word counted from the left: unbound noun roots of three and four underlying syllables stress the second syllable regularly (si'mori, ka'hap(o), a'sowa', e'rapoe'; e'panoki, mo'kovore), with the elided final /o/ still counting as a syllable; in verbs 'first stress is found on the second syllable if it is a syllable of the stem. Prefixes are extrametrical and do not get stressed' (p. 67); with a possessor proclitic the stress stays on the second syllable of the whole word (ni'kora, na'roni). Syllable weight overrides this: disyllabic nouns with a weak final vowel (/o/, weak /i/, which are elided or palatalised) stress the first = penultimate syllable ('hopi, 'him(o), 'tot(o)), while those with final /a/, /e/, strong /i/ or the diphthong /oe/ stress the second = final syllable (si'pa', si'ye', ko'hi'); a strong vowel /a/ in a suffix attracts stress (eto'nanev vs 'eton), and the plural suffix -nev is extrametrical while the locative -ye causes a stress shift on disyllables (hopi-'ye). Heavy syllables = those with strong /a/ or /e/, a glottalised (stressed) final vowel, or a closed syllable. Incorporated nouns can attract stress; monosyllabic classifiers stay unstressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'First of all, there is generally only one stress in a word. When the word is longer than four syllables there is secondary stress, which cannot occur on an adjacent syllable' (p. 64); 'Grammatical suffixes can get secondary stress, but generally when they contain a strong vowel /a/ or /e/ or when the syllable is pronounced as a closed syllable' (p. 67), e.g. na'soro,heyow (139) vs na'sorohew (140).
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllabic nouns split by final-vowel weight (as many first-stressed as second-stressed); heavy /a/ in the human plural -anev pulls stress to that syllable (eto'nanev); locative -ye shifts stress on disyllables; incorporated nouns may attract stress; phrase-level stress shift under vowel elision (p. 78–79: stress may shift, even onto a following closed syllable, in fast speech).
new_statements.identity_note: Danielsen 2007 describes Baure as spoken at Baures (Beni, Bolivia; fieldwork 2003–2006, cover photo from Baures 2006); Baptista & Wallin 1967: 27 locate their speakers on the Blanco, Negro and San Martín rivers, Province of Itenez, Department of Beni (5000 speakers then). Maggio 1749 is the Jesuit mission variety of the Moxos province. No work opened claims to describe the Carmelito or Joaquiniano varieties.

readall_conflicts: Maggio 1749 (in Adam & Leclerc 1880: 1; the catalog's existing statement) says stress is usually penultimate, quite often antepenultimate and sometimes final. Danielsen 2007: 64–67, the only modern phonological description opened, cites that statement and rejects it: stress is non-contrastive, the reliable generalisation is Baptista & Wallin's (1968) 'second syllable' (counted from the left, prefixes and the plural -nev extrametrical), and the residue is governed by syllable weight (weak final /o/ and weak /i/ push stress to the first syllable of disyllables; strong /a/, /e/, glottalised final vowels and closed syllables attract it), with secondary stress in words longer than four syllables. Baptista & Wallin 1967 is silent (no stress rule; marked forms only), and the 1965 Spanish version could not be opened. Admiraal 2016: 76 (held by the project from the earlier reading, not in this works list) speaks of primary stress on the locative noun stem 'usually penultimate syllable' in compounds, which fits Danielsen's disyllabic-stem case rather than a general penultimate rule. Net: the catalog's 'fixed: penultimate' rests only on the 1749 grammar and is superseded by Danielsen's second-syllable-plus-weight account; Maggio's three-way wording (penult / antepenult / final) is in fact what a left-edge second-syllable rule looks like from the right edge in 3-, 4- and 2-syllable words, so the two sources disagree on the analysis more than on the data.

tone.quote: 1.1 - INVENTARIO - Existen 18 fonemas segmentarios: doce consonantes [...] dos semiconsonantes: w, y, y cuatro vocales [...]. 1.4 - ACENTO - El acento es fonemico. El acento lexico ocurre mas frecuentemente en la segunda silaba: [roti] /roti/ "el", [noyonopa] /noyonopa/ "ellos van a ir". Sin embargo, en algunas palabras de dos silabas terminadas en vocal, el acento ocurre en la primera silaba [...]. Unas pocas veces ocurren dos o mas acentos en una palabra. [...] El acento lexicografico algunas veces queda interrumpido por el acento de entonacion que el enfasis y la armonia emocional del orador quiere comunicar
tone.locator: sec. 1.1 'Inventario', p. 9 and sec. 1.4 'Acento', pp. 12-13; example transcriptions simplified
tone.translation: 1.1 Inventory: There are 18 segmental phonemes: twelve consonants [...] two semiconsonants w, y, and four vowels [...]. 1.4 Accent: The accent is phonemic. Lexical accent occurs most frequently on the second syllable: /roti/ 'he', /noyonopa/ 'they are going to go'. However, in some two-syllable vowel-final words the accent falls on the first syllable [...]. Occasionally two or more accents occur in one word. [...] The lexical accent is sometimes interrupted by the intonational accent that the speaker's emphasis and emotional tone want to convey.
